text: Welcome to Designing Async Systems. The big shift is that a workflow can still look familiar at the business level, but once it moves into background workers, correctness depends on events, retries, ordering, and observability. So the question is: what has to become explicit when work moves across time?

A synchronous workflow moves to background workers, which improves responsiveness. The design pressure changes at the same time: correctness now depends on events, retries, ordering, and observability. The business workflow may look the same, but the execution model changes.

A useful way to reason about this is workflow, queue, worker, and evidence. The workflow submits work, the queue delivers it later, the worker acts later still, and the evidence logs what happened. Async design is about making the right thing happen across time and being able to defend it with evidence.

There are four core ideas here. Event storming makes significant events explicit. Workflow orchestration names the async control point. Error propagation has to work without a waiting user. Observability depends on correlation IDs and structured traces.

A design can pass once under ideal conditions and still be wrong. The hidden assumption is that the world will stay ordered, but timing changes quickly. Once pressure appears, the same operation can repeat, arrive late, or act on stale state. That is why the event boundary has to be explicit.

When async work gets more complex, the orchestrator becomes the control point that decides what happens next. It records the workflow, waits for results, and continues only when the right step is complete. The control logic is part of the design, and it makes the invariant visible.

Failure in the background is different from failure in a request-response flow. There may be no user waiting for an error, so the system has to survive crashes, retries, and redelivery. The protected property is safe recovery after partial failure, usually through idempotency, durable state, or another retry-safe handler design.

Observability is essential once work moves across workers and across time. Correlation IDs, structured logs, and traces connect a request to later events and prove the order of operations. For async systems, that evidence is part of the design, not an afterthought.

Start with the invariant, then choose the control. Once you know what must remain true, you can decide whether you need version checks, idempotency keys, durable completion records, retry with backoff, compensation, or reconciliation. Each control protects the invariant in a different way and adds its own cost.

A checkout flow makes the pattern concrete. The order event is published, the queue delivers it, the worker claims an idempotency key, and then the downstream notification happens. Duplicate delivery has to be harmless by design, not by luck.

The state transition path matters: enqueued, delivered, processing, completed, and acknowledged. That ordering protects the invariant that the external effect happens at most once, even if delivery happens more than once. The system proves discipline at the boundary or leaks correctness.

Make the failure uncomfortable: one worker ships the order, then crashes before acknowledgement, and the queue redelivers the same event to another worker. If delivery count and execution count are treated as the same thing, duplicate work or missing completion can follow. Structured evidence is what exposes the difference.

The corrected direction is to protect the invariant directly. Use idempotency keys, durable completion records, retry-safe handlers, and reconciliation where needed. That adds storage, bookkeeping, and handler complexity, but it is the cost of preventing duplicate side effects or lost completion.

This table is a comparison of controls under different pressure. A simple baseline is easy to explain, but it hides timing assumptions. Guarded transitions protect the invariant directly, but they need careful modeling. Explicit coordination makes dependencies visible, while idempotent retry-safe design handles queues and external calls with the right keys and deduplication.

To finish, treat async design like something you have to prove. Run the happy path, then the pressure path, and capture logs with IDs so you can compare before and after. Preserve the failing scenario and defend the fix with evidence.
